items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.

items.title: You can estimate pi by dropping a needle on a striped floor
items.claim: A floor has parallel lines spaced apart by distance L. Drop a needle of length L randomly. The probability the needle crosses a line is exactly 2/pi.
items.prompt: Why does pi appear in a problem with no circles?

options.text: The probability calculation involves integrating over the needle's random angle (a continuous variable on [0, pi]) and over its random position (linear), and the integral of sin theta from 0 to pi equals 2 — bringing pi into the denominator
Only works if the floor is circular

items.reveal:
Comte de Buffon set up the problem in 1733. Let d be the perpendicular distance from the needle's centre to the nearest line, and theta the angle the needle makes with the lines. The needle crosses a line if d is less than (L/2) sin theta.

Take d uniform on [0, L/2] and theta uniform on [0, pi/2]. Probability of crossing = (1 / (L/2 * pi/2)) * integral over the crossing region.

Working out: P = (2 / pi). So pi appears because the angle integration covers a full half-period of the sine.

This means you can estimate pi by dropping needles randomly: count crossings out of N drops, multiply by N/(2 * crossings) ≈ pi. Mario Lazzarini reported in 1901 having got pi to six decimals by 3408 throws — almost certainly cherry-picked (six decimals would require billions of throws).

Pi shows up in every probability problem involving a uniform-random angle. The constant of integration smuggles it in.
items.why: Pi is associated with circles. It actually appears in many problems involving angular randomness — anywhere a uniform integration over angles is required.
